# Fil-C: Memory-Safe C with Invisible Capabilities

## Thesis

**Fil-C** is a memory-safe implementation of C and C++ that keeps the languages you already write: clang extensions, atomics, threads, `mmap`, signals, even a large slice of inline assembly. Every pointer carries a **capability** that says which object it may touch and how. Out-of-bounds access, use-after-free, and capability corruption become **Fil-C panics**, not silent exploitation. There is no `unsafe` keyword and only limited FFI to unchecked code.

The engineering bet is *fanatical compatibility* on stock hardware (Linux x86_64 and ARM64). Pointers stay **64-bit** in the C address space; the capability lives in an invisible sidecar (InvisiCaps). As of **v0.686** (4 October 2026) the compiler is based on clang **20.1.8**. This chapter explains the capability model, why overhead is often acceptable (including the Fil-xz story), and a concrete byval/tail-padding bug that Anthropic helped fix — without installing Fil-C on this machine.

## Mental model

```text
  C program sees:     intval  (ordinary 64-bit pointer arithmetic / casts)
  Fil-C also keeps:   lower   (trusted object base + header)
                      upper   (exclusive end; lower==upper ⇒ no data access)
                      aux     (flags + pointer to aux capability table)

  flight pointer (in registers):  (lower, intval)
  rest pointer   (in the heap):   intval in payload;
                                  lower in aux allocation (or atomic box)
```

| Idea | Consequence |
|------|-------------|
| Capability, not tag | Hitting "valid memory" is not enough; the *pointer* must be allowed to that object (unlike ASan / MTE / HWAsan, which attackers can often bypass) |
| InvisiCaps | `sizeof(T*)` stays 8 on 64-bit; metadata is not in the C-visible object layout |
| Concurrent GC (FUGC) | `free` can deterministically disable all pointers to an object; UAF panics instead of corrupting capabilities |
| No `unsafe` | Safety is the ABI; escapes are limited FFI, not a keyword |
| Flight vs rest | Locals carry lower+intval; heap stores intval in the payload and lower in an aux page sized like the payload |

Compared with hardware capabilities (CHERI), InvisiCaps aim for similar enforcement while remaining binary-compatible with ordinary 64-bit pointers. Fil-C has iterated PLUT → SideCaps → MonoCaps → InvisiCaps; earlier models were slower, required knowing types at `malloc` time, or both.

## Worked examples

Fil-C is **not installed** on this box (no system package installs for scout runs). The cases below use ordinary gcc to show *what* Fil-C checks, and cite upstream docs for *how* Fil-C checks it. Version facts are from the Fil-C site and the v0.686 GitHub release notes (verified October 2026).

### Case 1: The bug class Fil-C turns into panics

```c
/* uaf_oob_demo.c — illustrates the class of errors Fil-C panics on.
 * Under Yolo-C (ordinary gcc/clang) these are undefined behaviour.
 * Under Fil-C, capability checks make them deterministic panics.
 * We do NOT run the buggy paths here; we only compile the safe skeleton. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
#include <string.h>

int main(void)
{
    char *p = malloc(4);
    if (!p) return 1;
    memcpy(p, "abcd", 4);

    /* SAFE: in-bounds write */
    p[3] = 'Z';
    printf("ok: %c%c%c%c\n", p[0], p[1], p[2], p[3]);

    /* Fil-C would panic on either of these (do not enable):
     *   p[4] = 'X';          // OOB — intval past upper
     *   free(p); p[0] = 'Y'; // UAF — free collapses upper to lower + free bit
     */
    free(p);
    return 0;
}
```

```bash
gcc -O2 -Wall -o uaf_oob_demo uaf_oob_demo.c
./uaf_oob_demo
```

```text
ok: abcZ
```

Under Fil-C, freeing sets the object's upper bound equal to lower and sets a free bit in the aux word, so a later load/store through any surviving pointer panics with a use-after-free diagnosis rather than reinterpreting recycled memory.

### Case 2: InvisiCaps at rest (why unions and atomics still work)

When a pointer is stored into the heap:

1. The **intval** lands in the object's payload (so integer loads see a normal address).
2. The **lower** lands in an **aux allocation** the same size as the payload (created lazily when the first pointer is stored).
3. Atomic / `volatile` / `std::atomic` pointer slots use 16-byte **atomic boxes** in the aux table so races cannot forge a capability — you may load the "wrong" valid lower, but not a corrupted one.

Objects with no pointers (strings, framebuffers) keep a NULL aux word: the GC treats them as leaves and space overhead stays far below 2×.

```text
  Object A payload:  [ ... | intval → B | ... ]
  Object A aux:      [ ... | lower_of_B | ... ]   ← invisible to C
  Object B header:   lower points here; upper = end of B
```

### Case 3: Fil-xz and the overhead story

Filip Pizło reports that **xz** has extremely low Fil-C overhead — low enough that Fil-xz is often competitive with, and sometimes faster than, a distro's older xz build, because xz's own algorithmic gains outweigh the safety tax. Upstream docs describe roughly **~1.5×** in good cases and up to about **~4×** in bad cases under InvisiCaps, with more optimisation headroom still open (calling convention, InvisiCap tuning, pointer chasing).

The practical takeaway for C engineers: measure *your* hot path. Compression, parsers, and other CPU-bound code with few pointer-heavy data structures are the optimistic region; pointer-chasing graphs are the pessimistic one.

### Case 4: Anthropic byval / tail-padding fix

Commit [`3485bcd`](https://github.com/pizlonator/fil-c/commit/3485bcdbc52605955993c6ff596b4794f5756850) (9 October 2026) fixed an uninitialized-memory issue in Fil-C's by-value argument path:

> the compiler [was] using a smaller size when *checking* byval arguments, and a larger size when *copying* them. This is due to the behavior of **tail padding**.

LLVM may copy a struct using its size *including* trailing padding, while capability checks used the logical (possibly smaller) size. The gap could leave padding bytes unchecked or copy past the capability. The commit message credits Anthropic with the bug report, almost all of the new tests (`byval-copy-test*`, `byval_tailpad_*`, misaligned demote cases), and most of the fix in `FilPizlonator.cpp` / `filc_runtime.c`.

Why it matters: Fil-C's calling convention copies arguments into thread-local payload and capability buffers with 8-byte rounding and alignment padding. Byval/byref edges are exactly where "invisible" metadata and ABI padding meet — a classic place for safety compilers to get the size wrong.

### Case 5: What v0.686 shipped

From the [v0.686 release notes](https://github.com/pizlonator/fil-c/releases/tag/v0.686) (4 October 2026), highlights include:

- Initial **C++ coroutine** support and limited `musttail` (may panic on stack overflow where Yolo-C would not)
- ARM64 GC / weak-load memory-ordering fixes
- fork(2) deadlocks with global init and exiting threads fixed
- Structs containing unions containing pointers as args/returns fixed
- `/opt/fil` package bumps (OpenSSL 3.6.5, xz 5.8.x line in the 0.685 rebase, etc.)

Download slices: self-contained **pizfix** tarballs (musl, no root) and **/opt/fil** (glibc, root) for x86_64 and ARM64.

## The trap

Treating Fil-C like AddressSanitizer. ASan finds bugs in tests; Fil-C is a **capability ABI** meant to stop exploitation in production. If you plan an `unsafe` escape hatch "just for this module", you are fighting the design — Fil-C deliberately has none. The other trap is installing a full Fil-C userland via apt/sudo on a shared scout box: use the documented pizfix tarball on a disposable machine, or read the docs and measure later.

## The boring rule

**Write normal C.** Prefer patterns Fil-C already runs (openssl, CPython, SQLite, OpenSSH in `/opt/fil`). When something panics, fix the memory error — do not reach for an unchecked FFI. For size/ABI surprises (byval, unions, tail padding), assume the capability size and the copy size must agree.

## Try this

1. On a disposable Linux VM, unpack `filc-0.686-linux-x86_64.tar.xz` from the GitHub release (no root required for pizfix) and rebuild a small project you own with `filcc`.
2. Deliberately add an OOB write and confirm you get a Fil-C panic with a useful origin, then remove it.
3. Read [InvisiCaps](https://fil-c.org/invisicaps) once end-to-end; sketch flight vs rest pointers from memory.
4. If you ship compression, compare wall time of distro `xz` vs a Fil-C build of current xz on *your* corpus before deciding overhead is unacceptable.
